newsitem.title: POLAND: Minister soothes Poles over Russia's NATO stance.
newsitem.headline: Minister soothes Poles over Russia's NATO stance.

text.p: Poland's foreign minister said on Thursday his country's NATO entry was on track despite Russian blustering and announced that he would visit Turkey partly to make clear that Ankara did not plan to block the process.
"I wish to assure everyone that this is all under control and going forward. There is no basis for unease that the established calendar will not be kept to," Dariusz Rosati said.
He was reacting to recent comments from Moscow officials repeating that Polish inclusion in NATO would threaten Russian security.
Warsaw, along with Prague and Budapest, expects to be invited at a NATO summit in Madrid in July to start entry negotiations and to become a full member by 1999.

Rosati produced a copy of a document signed by Boris Yeltsin in Warsaw in 1993 in which the Russian President recognised that a sovereign Poland's future membership of the pact would not be against Russia's interests.

"I want to stress that this clause, under which we have Yeltsin's signature, shows very clearly that at that stage Russia did not see the expansion of NATO by Poland as a factor threatening Russia's security," Rosati said.
"Let's not get too excited by all those signals coming from Russia," he said, adding these were either tactics in talks with the West or crafted for Russian internal politics.
Rosati said that next month he would visit Turkey, which has suggested it might block NATO enlargement unless it were given a green light to start negotiating for European Union membership.
He said he would seek assurances Turkey would not veto the entry of Poland and other countries, although the danger was not so bad as appeared from some public statements.
"But there is a need for a fundamental talk," he said.

He also announced that Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz would visit Brussels from February 19 to 21 to meet Belgian officials and also the heads of NATO, the European Commission and the Western European Union.

Rosati said Poland was being kept fully informed by its Western partners about their talks with Russia on their future relationship with Moscow, the alliance's enlargement and on the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, which Russia wants to revise.
Poland's Social Democratic (SdRP) party, dominant force in the ruling coalition, has suggested Poland should call a referendum on joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
Rosati said he personally thought this would be expensive and superfluous as Poles were clearly in favour.

A January opinion poll by public television's OBOP survey organisation showed on Thursday that 90 percent of Poles thought their country should strive to join NATO, and 88 percent said it should try to enter the EU.
